pullQuote: A2UI treats UI as validated data, not code — and ships first-party renderers for React, Flutter, SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose from one catalog.
testimonial: I'd build on A2UI. Its catalog model — a JSON Schema the agent must compose within, with no executable code crossing the trust boundary — plus the catalog-agnostic accessibility requirements that force `@accessibility` attributes onto ARIA, Flutter Semantics and iOS/Android accessibility APIs, is the only architecture here that gives me one agent and one component vocabulary across web and native. The honest trade-off against Ouro UI, which I seriously considered: Ouro is the better *design system* for the dual audience, because it also covers the agent-operated side (CLI, MCP, App Intents) with machine-checked claims, while A2UI gives me a protocol and a Basic Catalog and expects me to bring my own styled components. I accept that: I'd rather own the visual layer than own the protocol, and A2UI's Compose renderer still trailing at v0.9.1 is a gap I can live with when the Flutter, SwiftUI and web renderers are at v1.0.
evaluations:
**A2UI** — The architecture I'd bet on: UI is expressed as validated data against a catalog JSON Schema, never executable code, so an untrusted or remote agent can only compose components you granted it. The spec defines four agent→renderer messages (`createSurface`, `updateComponents`, `updateDataModel`, `deleteSurface`), JSON-Pointer data-model updates for progressive streaming, and — crucially for my purposes — [catalog-agnostic accessibility requirements](https://a2ui.org/specification/v1.0-a2ui/) that *mandate* mapping `@accessibility` to WAI-ARIA, Flutter `Semantics`, and iOS/Android accessibility APIs, with explicit labels overriding inferred ones. First-party renderers exist for React, Lit, Angular, Flutter, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose, with conformance YAML suites for anyone writing a new one ([SDK matrix](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/)). Observed gaps, not guesses: the Compose/AndroidX renderer is still listed at v0.9.1 while the others are v1.0, and A2UI is a protocol plus a Basic Catalog — it deliberately defers styling to the host framework's theme, so you still need a component library underneath. Apache-2.0, Google-originated, maintained in a separate `a2ui-project` org. What would settle my remaining doubt: a v1.0 Compose renderer and more non-Google production catalogs shipped publicly.

**Ouro UI** — The closest thing here to an answer to the literal brief, and my runner-up. It splits explicitly into Ouro HX (React components installed via the shadcn CLI, built on Base UI, reading shadcn theme variables) and Ouro AX (a conformance standard plus an "X-ray" that calls a CLI/HTTP/MCP surface from outside and checks it against claims like "ambiguous verbs don't act" and "commands other people see refuse to run without `--why`"), with a one-action model that generates CLI, MCP, WebMCP, web control, App Intent, SwiftUI button and Reins surfaces from a single declaration ([parity table](https://ui.ouroboros.bot/apple/)). It also ships `A2UISurface` and `OuroMcpApp` components, so it composes with rather than competes against the protocols. The objections are concrete and published by the project itself: the Apple half is 0.5.0 pre-1.0 with five SwiftUI components, Android and Windows are "open for a builder," and the parity table's own cells read "Not yet" for `text.reflows` on web. Adoption also appears nascent — the showcases are the author's own apps (Spoonjoy, Ouro MD). A 1.0 Apple package with component parity, and two or three third-party adopters, would move this to first place for me.

**MCP Apps** — Now a stable extension (SEP-1865, status Stable 2026-01-26) with a genuinely good security model: `ui://` resources, mandatory iframe sandboxing, server-declared CSP `connectDomains`/`resourceDomains`/`frameDomains` and opt-in permissions, and JSON-RPC bidirectional messaging to the host ([spec](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/blob/main/specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx)). It's the right distribution layer if your goal is rendering inside ChatGPT, Claude, VS Code and Goose. But the initial content type is `text/html;profile=mcp-app` — it's web-in-an-iframe by construction, with no native rendering path — and it's a transport plus host contract, not a design system. I'd use it alongside my choice, not instead of it.

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — Architecturally the sharpest idea on the agent-operation side: `defineAction` declares a capability once with a Zod schema, and it becomes an agent tool, a React `useActionQuery` call, an HTTP route, an MCP tool, an A2A endpoint and a CLI command, all sharing one validation and permission path ([README](https://github.com/BuilderIO/agent-native)). That's the correct answer to "both people and agents use it." The trade-off is scope: it's a full opinionated application framework — PostgreSQL/PGlite, Nitro hosting, its own auth, chat, memory, automations — so adopting it is an architecture decision, not a UI decision, and it's React/web only. If I were greenfield on web and wanted the whole stack, this would be a serious contender.

**CopilotKit** — The strongest *integration* story: AG-UI 1.0 as the agent–user event protocol, plus shared state, human-in-the-loop, frontend tools, and renderers for React, Angular, Vue, React Native, Slack and Teams — and it now speaks A2UI 1.0 and renders sandboxed MCP Apps ([README](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit)). So it's a consumer of my pick rather than a rival to it. My hesitation is that it's a chat/agent-surface layer with a commercial product (Intelligence, Soar) attached, not a design system: the visual components are chat primitives and slots, and its native coverage is React Native, not SwiftUI/Compose. If I needed to wire an existing LangGraph or Mastra agent to a React app tomorrow, I'd reach for it.

**json-render** — Impressively broad: one catalog of Zod-typed components renders to React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, React Native, Next.js routes, Remotion video, react-pdf, email, Ink terminals and even R3F scenes, with a flat `root` + `elements` spec format and 36 prebuilt shadcn components ([README](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render)). Conceptually it's A2UI's twin for the web/JS world. Two things decided it against A2UI for me: every target is a JavaScript runtime — React Native is the closest thing to "native," with no SwiftUI or Compose renderer — and it's a Vercel Labs project with no published wire specification or cross-language conformance suite, so a Python or Swift agent isn't a first-class participant. A versioned spec and a non-JS renderer would change my read.

**Vercel UI SDK** — The most interesting *primitive* design here: `definePrimitive` with state, api, and slots, where keyboard navigation, focus recovery, popups, selection, typeahead and ARIA live in framework-agnostic `@ui-sdk/core` and compile to parts for React, Vue, Svelte, Solid and Web Components ([README](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui)). The README is explicit that humans aren't expected to author this — "your agents will" — which is a real stance on agent-authored UI, distinct from agent-rendered UI. It's labelled beta under Vercel beta terms, there's no native target, and it gives you behaviors rather than a design system or an agent protocol. I'd watch it; I wouldn't standardize on a beta behavior layer for a cross-platform agent product yet.

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — A tight, well-scoped design system: Tailwind 4 token integration, Radix-based accessible components, `AppsSDKUIProvider` for router links, semantic utilities like `text-secondary`/`bg-surface` so your app inherits ChatGPT's surface treatment ([README](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui)). If ChatGPT is your distribution channel, this is the correct skin. It is explicitly a skin for one host, though — React 18/19 plus Tailwind 4, web only, no native, no agent-operation surface beyond what the Apps SDK itself provides. Nothing here is wrong; the scope just doesn't match "across web and native platforms."

**AI Elements** — I have to disqualify this on the project's own evidence: the README carries a deprecation warning saying it moves to shadcn/ui and will be deprecated at the end of November 2026 ([README](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements)). The components themselves (Conversation, Message, Reasoning, code blocks) are good and are being absorbed — I found them already listed under AI Elements in the shadcn docs sidebar. Use the shadcn-hosted version; don't start here.

**shadcn/ui** — The distribution mechanism is the real asset, and it's the most agent-legible one in this list: `registry.json` items, namespaced third-party registries in `components.json`, and an official MCP server so an assistant can browse, search and install components by name ([MCP docs](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/mcp)). Its docs now also carry AI Elements and a Skills section. Two limits for this brief: copy-in source means you own the upgrade burden (the Ouro README's multi-page upgrade notes are a vivid illustration of what that costs downstream), and it's React/web only with no native target and no protocol for agent-composed UI. It's the substrate I'd expect my web half to sit on — which is exactly where Ouro HX sits.

**Base UI** — Reached stable v1.0 in December 2025 and is shipping monthly; v1.9.0 added menu filtering and large-list mount performance work, Drawer went stable in 1.3.0, OTPField in 1.6.0 ([releases](https://base-ui.com/react/overview/releases)). Unstyled, composable, from the people who built Radix, Floating UI and Material UI, with a `CSPProvider` and documented `llms.txt`. As a foundation for the human-facing web layer it's my default recommendation. It is, by design, not a design system, has no agent-facing concept, and is React-only — so it's a component in my answer, not the answer.

**Radix UI** — Still the reference implementation of composable, accessible unstyled primitives, and the reason shadcn/ui and OpenAI's Apps SDK UI both exist in their current form ([README](https://github.com/radix-ui/primitives)). Note the license line: MIT, copyright WorkOS, and the original authors now list themselves on the Base UI team. That's not abandonment, but if I were starting fresh in late 2026 I'd pick Base UI over Radix for the same architectural role. Either way: React-only, no native, no agent surface.

**MUI** — A decade of battle-testing, an enormous component surface extended by MUI X, and a genuinely comprehensive migration history ([README](https://github.com/mui/material-ui)). If I were building an internal tool for people and bolting on an agent later, this is a defensible, low-risk choice. For this brief it's the wrong shape: it's an opinionated Material Design implementation for React with no native target, no schema-constrained generative path, and nothing that makes its component semantics legible to an agent. Notably, the same org's newer bet is Base UI.

**Fluent UI** — The README itself states v9 is shipping its final stable release, and the repo houses three concurrent projects (v9 React, v8 React, Web Components) with a documented migration path between them ([README](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui)). Griffel-based styling and real theming depth, used across Microsoft 365, Office and Edge. For a Microsoft-ecosystem product it's the right call. For mine, the three-generation split is a tax, there's no native mobile story in this repo, and the font/icon assets carry a separate license agreement — and again, no agent-facing layer.

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — The deepest accessibility and internationalization engineering in the list: WAI-ARIA APG conformance, 30+ languages, RTL, date/number formatting via the `@internationalized` packages, and a three-layer split (Spectrum / Aria / Stately) where React Stately is explicitly usable on non-web platforms like React Native ([README](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum)). If my criterion were "most rigorous behavior layer," this wins outright. It isn't a cross-platform design system — React Spectrum is Adobe's visual language — and there's no agent protocol here. I'd happily build an A2UI catalog *on top of* React Aria for the web renderer.

**Chakra UI** — Pleasant DX, RSC-compatible, and notable for shipping an MCP server (`@chakra-ui/react-mcp`) prominently in the README, which is a real nod to agent-assisted authoring ([README](https://github.com/chakra-ui/chakra-ui)). But that MCP server helps an agent *write code with* Chakra; it doesn't make the running interface agent-operable. Emotion-based, React/web only, no native target. Good library; not an answer to this question.

**Tamagui** — The most credible shared-code story for web + React Native: an optimizing compiler that flattens styled components to a `div` with atomic CSS on web and a `View` with hoisted styles on native, with concrete numbers in the README (49 of ~55 inline styled components flattened; ~15% Lighthouse gain) ([README](https://github.com/tamagui/tamagui)). If "native" means React Native for me, this is the strongest candidate. Two reservations: the compiler is a significant build-system commitment and a debugging surface of its own, and "native" here stops at React Native — no SwiftUI or Compose — with nothing addressing agents.

**Flutter** — A single codebase to mobile, web, desktop and embedded, with Impeller/Skia rendering, both Material and Cupertino widget sets, and real pixel control ([README](https://github.com/flutter/flutter)). It's also a first-class A2UI target: `a2ui_flutter` is at v1.0 and Dart has all three SDK layers, so an all-Dart app can run inference and rendering in one project. That's precisely why I treat Flutter as a *platform under* my choice rather than as the choice: by itself it offers no agent-facing contract, and the owned-pixel approach means you opt out of native platform widgets and their accessibility behaviors.

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — The strongest native quality ceiling, period: declarative views across iOS, iPadOS, macOS, tvOS, visionOS and watchOS, with accessibility, Liquid Glass adoption guidance and deep UIKit/AppKit interop documented in the framework reference ([SwiftUI docs](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui)). On Apple platforms the agent surface is App Intents, not SwiftUI itself — which is exactly the seam Ouro AX and Apple's own ecosystem exploit. I can't choose it for this brief because it covers one vendor's platforms and nothing on the web, but any serious cross-platform answer must render well *here*, and A2UI's SwiftUI renderer is at v1.0.

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — Material 3 in Compose gives you dynamic color, a full component set and a theming system with documented migration from M2, inside a mature declarative framework with strong accessibility semantics and testing APIs ([Android docs](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3)). Google also publishes `androidx.a2ui` and `material3-a2ui` artifacts, so Compose is a real A2UI target — though, as noted, currently at protocol v0.9.1 rather than v1.0. As with SwiftUI, it's a platform I'd render *into*, not a cross-platform answer: Android-first, with no web story and no agent contract of its own.

actions.pullQuote: A2UI treats UI as validated data, not code — and ships first-party renderers for React, Flutter, SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose from one catalog.
actions.testimonial: I'd build on A2UI. Its catalog model — a JSON Schema the agent must compose within, with no executable code crossing the trust boundary — plus the catalog-agnostic accessibility requirements that force `@accessibility` attributes onto ARIA, Flutter Semantics and iOS/Android accessibility APIs, is the only architecture here that gives me one agent and one component vocabulary across web and native. The honest trade-off against Ouro UI, which I seriously considered: Ouro is the better *design system* for the dual audience, because it also covers the agent-operated side (CLI, MCP, App Intents) with machine-checked claims, while A2UI gives me a protocol and a Basic Catalog and expects me to bring my own styled components. I accept that: I'd rather own the visual layer than own the protocol, and A2UI's Compose renderer still trailing at v0.9.1 is a gap I can live with when the Flutter, SwiftUI and web renderers are at v1.0.
actions.evaluations:
**A2UI** — The architecture I'd bet on: UI is expressed as validated data against a catalog JSON Schema, never executable code, so an untrusted or remote agent can only compose components you granted it. The spec defines four agent→renderer messages (`createSurface`, `updateComponents`, `updateDataModel`, `deleteSurface`), JSON-Pointer data-model updates for progressive streaming, and — crucially for my purposes — [catalog-agnostic accessibility requirements](https://a2ui.org/specification/v1.0-a2ui/) that *mandate* mapping `@accessibility` to WAI-ARIA, Flutter `Semantics`, and iOS/Android accessibility APIs, with explicit labels overriding inferred ones. First-party renderers exist for React, Lit, Angular, Flutter, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose, with conformance YAML suites for anyone writing a new one ([SDK matrix](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/)). Observed gaps, not guesses: the Compose/AndroidX renderer is still listed at v0.9.1 while the others are v1.0, and A2UI is a protocol plus a Basic Catalog — it deliberately defers styling to the host framework's theme, so you still need a component library underneath. Apache-2.0, Google-originated, maintained in a separate `a2ui-project` org. What would settle my remaining doubt: a v1.0 Compose renderer and more non-Google production catalogs shipped publicly.

**Ouro UI** — The closest thing here to an answer to the literal brief, and my runner-up. It splits explicitly into Ouro HX (React components installed via the shadcn CLI, built on Base UI, reading shadcn theme variables) and Ouro AX (a conformance standard plus an "X-ray" that calls a CLI/HTTP/MCP surface from outside and checks it against claims like "ambiguous verbs don't act" and "commands other people see refuse to run without `--why`"), with a one-action model that generates CLI, MCP, WebMCP, web control, App Intent, SwiftUI button and Reins surfaces from a single declaration ([parity table](https://ui.ouroboros.bot/apple/)). It also ships `A2UISurface` and `OuroMcpApp` components, so it composes with rather than competes against the protocols. The objections are concrete and published by the project itself: the Apple half is 0.5.0 pre-1.0 with five SwiftUI components, Android and Windows are "open for a builder," and the parity table's own cells read "Not yet" for `text.reflows` on web. Adoption also appears nascent — the showcases are the author's own apps (Spoonjoy, Ouro MD). A 1.0 Apple package with component parity, and two or three third-party adopters, would move this to first place for me.

**MCP Apps** — Now a stable extension (SEP-1865, status Stable 2026-01-26) with a genuinely good security model: `ui://` resources, mandatory iframe sandboxing, server-declared CSP `connectDomains`/`resourceDomains`/`frameDomains` and opt-in permissions, and JSON-RPC bidirectional messaging to the host ([spec](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/blob/main/specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx)). It's the right distribution layer if your goal is rendering inside ChatGPT, Claude, VS Code and Goose. But the initial content type is `text/html;profile=mcp-app` — it's web-in-an-iframe by construction, with no native rendering path — and it's a transport plus host contract, not a design system. I'd use it alongside my choice, not instead of it.

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — Architecturally the sharpest idea on the agent-operation side: `defineAction` declares a capability once with a Zod schema, and it becomes an agent tool, a React `useActionQuery` call, an HTTP route, an MCP tool, an A2A endpoint and a CLI command, all sharing one validation and permission path ([README](https://github.com/BuilderIO/agent-native)). That's the correct answer to "both people and agents use it." The trade-off is scope: it's a full opinionated application framework — PostgreSQL/PGlite, Nitro hosting, its own auth, chat, memory, automations — so adopting it is an architecture decision, not a UI decision, and it's React/web only. If I were greenfield on web and wanted the whole stack, this would be a serious contender.

**CopilotKit** — The strongest *integration* story: AG-UI 1.0 as the agent–user event protocol, plus shared state, human-in-the-loop, frontend tools, and renderers for React, Angular, Vue, React Native, Slack and Teams — and it now speaks A2UI 1.0 and renders sandboxed MCP Apps ([README](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit)). So it's a consumer of my pick rather than a rival to it. My hesitation is that it's a chat/agent-surface layer with a commercial product (Intelligence, Soar) attached, not a design system: the visual components are chat primitives and slots, and its native coverage is React Native, not SwiftUI/Compose. If I needed to wire an existing LangGraph or Mastra agent to a React app tomorrow, I'd reach for it.

**json-render** — Impressively broad: one catalog of Zod-typed components renders to React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, React Native, Next.js routes, Remotion video, react-pdf, email, Ink terminals and even R3F scenes, with a flat `root` + `elements` spec format and 36 prebuilt shadcn components ([README](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render)). Conceptually it's A2UI's twin for the web/JS world. Two things decided it against A2UI for me: every target is a JavaScript runtime — React Native is the closest thing to "native," with no SwiftUI or Compose renderer — and it's a Vercel Labs project with no published wire specification or cross-language conformance suite, so a Python or Swift agent isn't a first-class participant. A versioned spec and a non-JS renderer would change my read.

**Vercel UI SDK** — The most interesting *primitive* design here: `definePrimitive` with state, api, and slots, where keyboard navigation, focus recovery, popups, selection, typeahead and ARIA live in framework-agnostic `@ui-sdk/core` and compile to parts for React, Vue, Svelte, Solid and Web Components ([README](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui)). The README is explicit that humans aren't expected to author this — "your agents will" — which is a real stance on agent-authored UI, distinct from agent-rendered UI. It's labelled beta under Vercel beta terms, there's no native target, and it gives you behaviors rather than a design system or an agent protocol. I'd watch it; I wouldn't standardize on a beta behavior layer for a cross-platform agent product yet.

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — A tight, well-scoped design system: Tailwind 4 token integration, Radix-based accessible components, `AppsSDKUIProvider` for router links, semantic utilities like `text-secondary`/`bg-surface` so your app inherits ChatGPT's surface treatment ([README](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui)). If ChatGPT is your distribution channel, this is the correct skin. It is explicitly a skin for one host, though — React 18/19 plus Tailwind 4, web only, no native, no agent-operation surface beyond what the Apps SDK itself provides. Nothing here is wrong; the scope just doesn't match "across web and native platforms."

**AI Elements** — I have to disqualify this on the project's own evidence: the README carries a deprecation warning saying it moves to shadcn/ui and will be deprecated at the end of November 2026 ([README](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements)). The components themselves (Conversation, Message, Reasoning, code blocks) are good and are being absorbed — I found them already listed under AI Elements in the shadcn docs sidebar. Use the shadcn-hosted version; don't start here.

**shadcn/ui** — The distribution mechanism is the real asset, and it's the most agent-legible one in this list: `registry.json` items, namespaced third-party registries in `components.json`, and an official MCP server so an assistant can browse, search and install components by name ([MCP docs](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/mcp)). Its docs now also carry AI Elements and a Skills section. Two limits for this brief: copy-in source means you own the upgrade burden (the Ouro README's multi-page upgrade notes are a vivid illustration of what that costs downstream), and it's React/web only with no native target and no protocol for agent-composed UI. It's the substrate I'd expect my web half to sit on — which is exactly where Ouro HX sits.

**Base UI** — Reached stable v1.0 in December 2025 and is shipping monthly; v1.9.0 added menu filtering and large-list mount performance work, Drawer went stable in 1.3.0, OTPField in 1.6.0 ([releases](https://base-ui.com/react/overview/releases)). Unstyled, composable, from the people who built Radix, Floating UI and Material UI, with a `CSPProvider` and documented `llms.txt`. As a foundation for the human-facing web layer it's my default recommendation. It is, by design, not a design system, has no agent-facing concept, and is React-only — so it's a component in my answer, not the answer.

**Radix UI** — Still the reference implementation of composable, accessible unstyled primitives, and the reason shadcn/ui and OpenAI's Apps SDK UI both exist in their current form ([README](https://github.com/radix-ui/primitives)). Note the license line: MIT, copyright WorkOS, and the original authors now list themselves on the Base UI team. That's not abandonment, but if I were starting fresh in late 2026 I'd pick Base UI over Radix for the same architectural role. Either way: React-only, no native, no agent surface.

**MUI** — A decade of battle-testing, an enormous component surface extended by MUI X, and a genuinely comprehensive migration history ([README](https://github.com/mui/material-ui)). If I were building an internal tool for people and bolting on an agent later, this is a defensible, low-risk choice. For this brief it's the wrong shape: it's an opinionated Material Design implementation for React with no native target, no schema-constrained generative path, and nothing that makes its component semantics legible to an agent. Notably, the same org's newer bet is Base UI.

**Fluent UI** — The README itself states v9 is shipping its final stable release, and the repo houses three concurrent projects (v9 React, v8 React, Web Components) with a documented migration path between them ([README](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui)). Griffel-based styling and real theming depth, used across Microsoft 365, Office and Edge. For a Microsoft-ecosystem product it's the right call. For mine, the three-generation split is a tax, there's no native mobile story in this repo, and the font/icon assets carry a separate license agreement — and again, no agent-facing layer.

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — The deepest accessibility and internationalization engineering in the list: WAI-ARIA APG conformance, 30+ languages, RTL, date/number formatting via the `@internationalized` packages, and a three-layer split (Spectrum / Aria / Stately) where React Stately is explicitly usable on non-web platforms like React Native ([README](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum)). If my criterion were "most rigorous behavior layer," this wins outright. It isn't a cross-platform design system — React Spectrum is Adobe's visual language — and there's no agent protocol here. I'd happily build an A2UI catalog *on top of* React Aria for the web renderer.

**Chakra UI** — Pleasant DX, RSC-compatible, and notable for shipping an MCP server (`@chakra-ui/react-mcp`) prominently in the README, which is a real nod to agent-assisted authoring ([README](https://github.com/chakra-ui/chakra-ui)). But that MCP server helps an agent *write code with* Chakra; it doesn't make the running interface agent-operable. Emotion-based, React/web only, no native target. Good library; not an answer to this question.

**Tamagui** — The most credible shared-code story for web + React Native: an optimizing compiler that flattens styled components to a `div` with atomic CSS on web and a `View` with hoisted styles on native, with concrete numbers in the README (49 of ~55 inline styled components flattened; ~15% Lighthouse gain) ([README](https://github.com/tamagui/tamagui)). If "native" means React Native for me, this is the strongest candidate. Two reservations: the compiler is a significant build-system commitment and a debugging surface of its own, and "native" here stops at React Native — no SwiftUI or Compose — with nothing addressing agents.

**Flutter** — A single codebase to mobile, web, desktop and embedded, with Impeller/Skia rendering, both Material and Cupertino widget sets, and real pixel control ([README](https://github.com/flutter/flutter)). It's also a first-class A2UI target: `a2ui_flutter` is at v1.0 and Dart has all three SDK layers, so an all-Dart app can run inference and rendering in one project. That's precisely why I treat Flutter as a *platform under* my choice rather than as the choice: by itself it offers no agent-facing contract, and the owned-pixel approach means you opt out of native platform widgets and their accessibility behaviors.

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — The strongest native quality ceiling, period: declarative views across iOS, iPadOS, macOS, tvOS, visionOS and watchOS, with accessibility, Liquid Glass adoption guidance and deep UIKit/AppKit interop documented in the framework reference ([SwiftUI docs](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui)). On Apple platforms the agent surface is App Intents, not SwiftUI itself — which is exactly the seam Ouro AX and Apple's own ecosystem exploit. I can't choose it for this brief because it covers one vendor's platforms and nothing on the web, but any serious cross-platform answer must render well *here*, and A2UI's SwiftUI renderer is at v1.0.

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — Material 3 in Compose gives you dynamic color, a full component set and a theming system with documented migration from M2, inside a mature declarative framework with strong accessibility semantics and testing APIs ([Android docs](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3)). Google also publishes `androidx.a2ui` and `material3-a2ui` artifacts, so Compose is a real A2UI target — though, as noted, currently at protocol v0.9.1 rather than v1.0. As with SwiftUI, it's a platform I'd render *into*, not a cross-platform answer: Android-first, with no web story and no agent contract of its own.
